Jane Austen wrote six novels, which feels like a small number considering how often her work pops up in a contemporary setting. Her books have been adapted into prestige films, miniseries, loose Hollywood reimaginings, and at least one zombie mashup. They've shaped how novelists from the Brontës to Sally Rooney think about interiority and dialogue, and the way two people in a room can say one thing and mean another. Even unfinished fragments like Sanditon and The Watsons have made their way mainstream.

Readers don't just like these books, they feel ownership over them, which is why ranking them almost always sparks a fight in the comments section. We're issuing that warning now because, yes, we did assign numbers. And yes, you will have feelings about what ends up where on the list below.

Catherine Morland is seventeen, sheltered, and an absolute fiend for Gothic novels. When a family friend brings her to Bath for the social season, she falls in with two very different crowds: the Thorpes, who are loud and scheming, and the Tilneys, who are warm, witty, and very much Catherine's speed. She develops feelings for Henry Tilney, the clergyman son, and he seems to return them. But, when his father invites her to their estate, Northanger Abbey, Catherine arrives expecting something out of The Mysteries of Udolpho. Basically, she lets her imagination run completely off the rails and almost ruins everything.

The novel was written in the late 1790s, sold to a publisher in 1803, and didn't see print until 1817, after Austen's death, which means it's simultaneously her youngest book and her most delayed. You can feel it. The satire of Gothic fiction is sharp and very funny, and Catherine's naivety makes her one of Austen's most endearing heroines, but the novel lacks the layered psychology Austen brought to her later work. Henry Tilney is charming enough, though he has a tendency to lecture, and the plot wraps itself up with a speed that suggests Austen had other ideas she wanted to get to. It lands at the bottom because it's Austen still figuring out what she could do with a story.

Austen's first published novel gets treated like a warm-up act for the rest of her work, and within the first hundred pages or so, you can see why. The premise is deceptively simple: two sisters who process the same disaster in completely different ways. Elinor Dashwood is steady and private. Marianne Dashwood feels everything at full volume. After their father's death strips the family of their home and income, they relocate to a small cottage in Devon, and Marianne throws herself into a romance with John Willoughby, a charming man she meets after tumbling down a hill in a rainstorm. Elinor is also in love with Edward Ferrars, but she'd rather die than make a scene about it.

Then Sense and Sensibility gets mean. Willoughby's exit is brutal. Lucy Steele's secret engagement to Edward is a gut punch. The tidy set-up cracks open and what's underneath is a novel about what it costs women to have feelings in a world that will punish them for it. By the time Marianne falls dangerously ill, you're fully in it. And even though Austen wraps the love interests up almost suspiciously fast at the end, you don't care because you've spent the whole book worrying about these two women, and you're just glad they're okay.

Nobody agrees about this one, and they haven't since it was published in 1814. Mansfield Park is the Austen novel that splits readers down the middle, and where you end up on the fault line is almost always because of your feelings about Fanny Price. She's a shy, morally serious girl who gets shipped from her parents' chaotic house in Portsmouth to live with her wealthy uncle's family at age ten. The Bertrams take her in, but only Edmund, the younger son, treats her like she belongs. Fanny grows up grateful and overlooked, quietly in love with Edmund and increasingly invisible to everyone else. When the glamorous Crawford siblings show up and start charming the household into chaos, Fanny is the only person who can see through them.

She watches Henry Crawford toy with the Bertram sisters. She watches Mary Crawford's wit pull Edmund in. Fanny says almost nothing about either, which is admirable or frustrating depending on your preference. That's the gamble of this novel. It doesn't give you the pleasure of rooting for someone bold, but it does get you to notice how someone's principles can cost them almost everything.

How do you usually end up making a new friend?
The origin story says a lot about the friendship that follows it.

AWe got loud about the same obsession and never stopped.
BThey invited me somewhere before we had properly met.
CWe bonded over disliking exactly the same thing.
DThey noticed I was struggling and stayed with me.

What is a perfect Saturday with your best friend?
Friendship is mostly built out of very ordinary hours.

AA ridiculous plan neither of us should attempt.
BSomewhere new, photographed heavily, ending very late.
CSomewhere quiet, few people, zero small talk.
DSomething simple, and a conversation that actually matters.

This is the real test of a friendship, and everybody knows it.

AThey are already putting their shoes on.
BThey answer instantly and turn it into a plan.
CThey answer and say something unflattering and true.
DThey listen for an hour and never check the time.

What do you want from them when you are clearly wrong?
The best friendships are the ones that survive being corrected.

ASupport first. We can review the mistake later.
BA relentlessly positive reframe of the entire disaster.
CThe blunt version. Do not soften it for me.
DPatience, and no judgment about how I got here.

What do your friends actually value about you?
The friend you attract says something about the friend you are.

AI am all in, always, about everything.
BI can turn almost any situation into a good time.
CI say the thing nobody else in the room will.
DI look after whoever is having the worst day.

How a friendship repairs itself matters more than how it breaks.

ALoudly, briefly, then back to normal by Tuesday.
BThey apologise first, enthusiastically, with a gift.
CCold silence, then one dry joke that fixes everything.
DWe talk until we both understand what actually happened.

CTo catch me when I start lying to myself.
DTo be the person who never gave up on me.

Ten years from now, what keeps the two of you close?

AWe would still drop everything for each other, instantly.
BWe still make plans, and we still actually go.
CWe still cut through each other's nonsense in one sentence.
DThey stood by me once when it cost them something.
